summary.text: 假 combines the person side-form 亻 with 叚, conventionally analyzed as its sound component. The character is used for “false” and “borrow,” but the relationship and order of those meanings remain unresolved.

formation.text: The traditional analysis treats 假 as phonosemantic: 亻 contributes a person-related meaning, while 叚 supplies a sound cue. A competing proposal treats 人 as an addition distinguishing 假 from 叚 in Qin-period writing; this does not settle how the two meanings of 假 developed.

components.text: 亻 is the side form of 人. In the traditional analysis, it contributes a person-related meaning; another proposal treats 人 as a graphic addition distinguishing 假 from 叚.
叚 is conventionally analyzed as the phonetic component. The descriptions of its bronze forms concern 叚 itself and do not establish a graphic sequence for 假.

sound_limitation.text: The historical comparison supports the proposed sound relation for the “borrow; false” reading, but not for every reading of 假.

sound.text: Modern Mandarin lists both 叚 and 假 with the reading jiǎ; this current match alone does not establish their ancient sound relationship.
In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese notation, 叚 and 假 in the “borrow; false” reading share the reconstruction *Cə.kˤraʔ; the same dataset gives another reconstruction for a different reading of 假.

history.text: A scholarly account reports 叚 in excavated pre-Qin texts and 假 in Qin-period documents. It interprets a document dated to 221 BCE as distinguishing 叚 for lending from 假 for borrowing, and proposes that 人 was added to distinguish the written forms. This is one account of the evidence.
Later texts are reported to mix the spellings 叚 and 假. The available accounts do not trace a dated sequence of 假’s later graphic changes.

Descriptions of 叚’s bronze forms identify 爪, 又, and 石 as graphic elements and list uses read as “blessing,” “fault,” interrogative words, and others. This account concerns 叚, not an evolutionary path for 假.

uncertainties.text: The traditional analysis assigns 亻 a semantic role and 叚 a phonetic role; another proposal treats 人 as a graphic addition distinguishing 假 from 叚. The accounts do not resolve how these explanations relate.
The proposed development from “borrow” through “simulate” to “false” is disputed; the cited accounts do not establish a dated link between borrowing and falsehood.
A historical sound comparison is available for one reading of 假, but the evidence does not show that it applies to every reading.

senses.text: 假 is glossed as “not true,” and a cited classical example uses it to mean “false” or “not so.” The example’s date and status as the earliest attestation are unresolved.

senses.period: classical text; composition and attestation dating unresolved
senses.text: A cited classical example uses 假 for borrowing a passage. A scholarly account interprets Qin-period writing as distinguishing 假 for borrowing from 叚 for lending; this does not show that borrowing was the earlier meaning of 假.

senses.period: historical and current; first attestation unresolved
senses.text: Textual examples record temporary or acting uses, and modern definitions include “vacation.” Their dates and relationship to “borrow” or “false” are unresolved.

limitations.text: The cited senses do not establish their relative chronology or a continuous semantic development. In particular, the proposed path from borrowing through simulation to falsehood remains disputed.

overview.text: 假 combines 亻, the side form of 人, with 叚 as a sound component. It is used for “false” and “borrow,” but how those meanings are connected is unresolved.

components.text: 亻 is the side form of 人; in the traditional analysis, it contributes a person-related meaning.
叚 is conventionally treated as the sound component. The comparisons support particular readings, not every use of 假.

relationships.text: In the traditional analysis of 假, 亻 contributes a person-related meaning; another account treats 人 as a graphic addition distinguishing 假 from 叚.
The traditional analysis assigns 叚 the sound role. Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstructions match 叚 with one reading of 假, but do not establish the role for every reading.
